dataset.probe_query: SELECT id, name FROM lab_index_probe WHERE email = 'user37777@example.com'

verified_behaviors: Without a secondary index the equality query plans as type=ALL and actually reads 50,001 rows (Handler_read_rnd_next) over 50,000 rows; EXPLAIN ANALYZE reports actual time 19.8..26.1 ms
Adding idx_email turns the plan into type=ref/key=idx_email with Handler_read_next=1, and the 5-run median wall time drops from 23.451 ms to 0.713 ms (32.9x)
A composite idx_email_name (email, name) produces Extra=Using index (covering), median 0.965 ms, Handler_read_key=1 and no table lookup
A prefix LIKE query uses type=range on idx_email_name, reading only 11 rows (Extra=Using where; Using index)
With innodb_deadlock_detect=ON the opposite-order update pair produces MySQL error 1213 (deadlock) on one session after 1015 ms while the other commits
With innodb_deadlock_detect=OFF the same workload produces error 1205 (lock wait timeout) on BOTH sessions after ~5868 ms with innodb_lock_wait_timeout=5, and no 1213 at all

innodb_deadlock_detect is a GLOBAL-only variable in 8.4 (SET SESSION fails with 1229); the probe therefore flips it server-wide and restores it to ON afterwards (verified: @@global.innodb_deadlock_detect=1)
limitations: Single instance, no replication or crash recovery drill
Timing is a local warm-buffer single-instance measurement, not a capacity result
The deadlock-detection switch is a server-global variable, so the OFF run affects every session on that instance
No slow-query-log or optimizer-trace analysis was performed; conclusions come from EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE / Handler counters
